threads.thread_goal: Align on pilot scope, roles and initial household targeting approach.

messages.text: Kicking off the Community Food Support and Outreach Pilot here. I have shared the overview doc for this 6‑week pilot (see project_pack_ref: Community Food Support and Outreach Pilot and A1). The aim is to combine surplus food redistribution with short doorstep check‑ins. From my side, I am seeing three core pieces: 1) clarity on the pilot objective and what success looks like, 2) who does what across T1 and T5, and 3) an initial approach to identifying target households. Can you all take a look and share any concerns or suggestions on scope and roles before we lock this down?

Thanks for starting this. From reading A1, the objective sounds like: reduce food waste while reaching residents who might not be in touch with services. For success criteria, I would suggest we track at least: number of households reached weekly, number of successful deliveries vs attempted, and a light sense of whether people feel the support is useful. On roles, I am happy to support T1 alongside you, especially on documenting eligibility and making sure we use anonymised IDs from the start.

From an operations angle, the 6‑week limit in the overview is tight but workable if we keep the first week lighter. For scope, it would help me if we define an approximate upper limit of households early, so I can later align production and packing capacity with T2 and T3. I do not need exact addresses yet, just a ballpark and any constraints like maximum parcels per day.

On the delivery side, I am wondering how many stops per route we are thinking about. My regular round already has fixed timings, so I need to understand if we are adding, say, 5 or 20 households. Also, for the doorstep check‑ins, will we have a script ready from T5 before we start, or do we test something informal first?

For targeting households, once T1 gives us anonymised IDs, I can later plug those into the tracking sheet linked to A5 and A6. That means we should avoid collecting more personal data than needed from the start. For scope, I would suggest we start with a modest number, maybe around 30–40 households total, then see if we can scale within the 6 weeks.

Good questions. My proposal for the objective, based on A1 and what you all said, is: over 6 weeks, provide weekly surplus food parcels and a brief wellbeing check to a defined group of households, while testing a safe and repeatable process. Success would be: 1) at least 80 percent of planned deliveries completed each week, 2) no food safety incidents, and 3) positive or neutral feedback from most households on the doorstep interaction. Does anyone see gaps or risks with that framing before we confirm it?

From my side, those success points are workable. I would just add that we should explicitly track any near‑misses in the operational issues log later (A7), even if they are not full incidents. That will help us refine processes before scaling. Otherwise, the objective sounds clear enough for me to plan T2 and T3 around it.

I like that framing. To keep it realistic for doorstep conversations, maybe we phrase the third success point as: most households are comfortable with the visit and at least some report that the support is helpful. We can capture that in a simple rating or short note later in A6. With that tweak, I am comfortable saying this is our pilot objective.

Agreed, let us lock that in. Summarising: for 6 weeks we will deliver weekly surplus food parcels and a short wellbeing check to a defined group of households, aiming for high completion of planned deliveries, no food safety incidents, and households generally feeling comfortable and supported. I will treat that as our confirmed pilot objective and success criteria and reflect it in A1.

On eligibility for T1, I suggest we prioritise: 1) households already known to the community social work team as experiencing food insecurity or isolation, 2) older adults living alone, and 3) families with young children referred by local organisations. We should also include a simple opt‑in step via partners so people know what to expect and can decline. In terms of numbers, starting with around 30–35 households feels manageable for the first cycle.

If we are talking about 30–35 households, that sounds more realistic for fitting into existing routes. I would still prefer if we cluster them into 2 or 3 route groups rather than spreading them thinly. That way, I can add a small block of stops to certain days instead of lots of single extra stops. Could we also avoid very late‑evening visits, as that tends to clash with my current schedule?

For anonymised IDs in T1, I propose a simple code: area code plus sequential number, for example, N1‑001. That will work well with A5 later and avoids names or full addresses in shared sheets. We can keep the mapping to real addresses in a separate, restricted file outside this channel.

Clustering into 2–3 route groups works for me. If we cap at around 12–15 households per route day, I can plan packing volumes and timing. That would keep the total around 30–35 households as suggested. We just need to be clear that we are not promising more than one delivery per week per household during the pilot.

Let me summarise the eligibility and numbers so we can confirm. Proposal: 1) focus on households already known to services or referred by trusted community partners as facing food insecurity or isolation, 2) prioritise older adults living alone and families with young children, 3) use an opt‑in approach via partners, and 4) start with approximately 30–35 households, grouped into 2–3 route clusters. If there are no strong objections, I will treat this as our agreed scope for T1.
That summary matches what I had in mind. I can start drafting the eligibility note and initial anonymised list for T1 based on those points, then loop in community partners to confirm feasibility.

Great, then we will go ahead with that. Decision for the record: the pilot will target roughly 30–35 households, prioritising those already known or referred as facing food insecurity or isolation, with opt‑in via partners and anonymised IDs as per T1. I will update A1 accordingly and start planning T9 so everyone is briefed on this scope.

Once the anonymised list is ready from T1, please share the household codes and route clusters. I will prepare a first draft of the tracking layout in line with A5 and A6 so we can test it during the dry run later.

Thanks for clarifying the numbers and clusters. Once we have the draft routes from T4, I would like to review them against my current round to flag any timing issues early, especially around late‑evening slots.

threads.thread_goal: Design and agree on the end-to-end operational flow from surplus collection to delivery.

messages.text: Starting an operations thread to map the flow from surplus collection to doorstep. Based on the pilot overview and my first draft for T2, here is a simple proposal: 1) collect surplus from store and warehouse at set times, 2) sort and check items against A2 guidance, 3) pack parcels using the structure in A3 and T6, 4) stage parcels by route, and 5) hand over to delivery with a quick check against the route list from T4. Can you review this flow and highlight anything missing or unrealistic?

Flow looks sensible. For T6, I suggest we structure the packing checklist around: 1) base items (staples), 2) fresh items with clear expiry checks, and 3) optional extras if available. We should also include a quick visual check that packaging is intact. That will make it easier for volunteers to follow without needing detailed training.

On the handover step, could we keep the paperwork or digital checks as light as possible? If I have to sign multiple forms at each pickup, it will slow down the route. Maybe a single route sheet from T4 with household codes and a tick box for each parcel would be enough.

We can definitely keep it simple. I can align the route sheet with A5 so that for each route you just have household codes, a parcel count, and a tick column. That way, we avoid extra forms and still have enough traceability for A6 later.

From a community side, I just want to flag that delays at any step could mean doorstep visits happening too late in the day, which might not be comfortable for some households. Could we build in a buffer between packing and dispatch, and maybe set a latest delivery time per route?

Good point. If we fix collection and sorting in the morning, we can aim to finish packing by early afternoon, leaving a buffer before dispatch. For example: 1) collection 9–10, 2) sorting and checks 10–12, 3) packing 12–14, 4) dispatch 14–17 with a latest doorstep time of 17:30. Does that fit with your existing rounds?

Those times could work if we align the pilot routes with my lighter days. I would prefer to avoid Fridays, which are usually the heaviest. If we can keep most pilot deliveries to two mid‑week afternoons, I should be able to fit them in without rushing the doorstep conversations.

For the sorting step in T2, can we be explicit that anything not meeting A2 standards is removed before it reaches the packing area? That will keep the T6 checklist focused on parcels that are already safe, rather than asking packers to make complex decisions.

Yes, that makes sense. I will structure T2 so that sorting includes a clear pass or reject step based on A2, and only passed items move to the packing area. T6 can then focus on quantities, variety, and final expiry checks.

One more suggestion: at the staging step, we can label each parcel with the household code and route code, using the scheme we will define in T7. That way, when parcels are loaded, it is easy to see which ones belong to which route, and we reduce the risk of mix‑ups.
That labelling will also help if we need to record any missed deliveries in A7 later. If a parcel cannot be delivered, we can log the household code and reason without using names.

Let me summarise the standard process so far: 1) scheduled surplus collection from store and warehouse, 2) centralised sorting with a clear pass or reject step using A2, 3) packing parcels following A3 and T6, 4) staging parcels by route with labels from T7, and 5) handover to delivery using a simple route sheet aligned with T4 and A5, with deliveries mainly on two mid‑week afternoons and a latest doorstep time of around 17:30. If everyone is comfortable with this, I will treat it as our agreed standard flow for the pilot.
That summary captures the key steps clearly. From the packing side, I am happy to work with that as the standard process and will reflect it when drafting T6.

I am ok with that flow and the timing, as long as we keep the two mid‑week afternoons and avoid Fridays. For route ownership in T4, I can take the two main pilot routes, but if we add a third route later we might need another driver or to split it across days.

To close the loop on schedule and route ownership: proposal is that we run two main routes on mid‑week afternoons, both owned by you for the pilot, with a possible small third cluster only if we see capacity. We will avoid Fridays and late‑evening deliveries. If no one objects, we can confirm this as the delivery schedule for T4.
Works for me. Having two fixed mid‑week routes will make it easier to plan production and packing windows consistently across the 6 weeks.
I will set up the route codes in A5 to match those two mid‑week routes so that tracking and logging in A6 line up with what you have just agreed.

threads.thread_goal: Finalise safety, privacy and doorstep interaction guidelines.

messages.text: I have drafted a short food safety and hygiene guide for the pilot based on A2 and the requirements in T3. It covers hand hygiene, temperature control, separation of raw and ready‑to‑eat items, and what to do if there is any doubt about an item. In parallel, there is a first version of the doorstep script for T5, aligned with A4. Can you review both and flag anything that feels unclear or too heavy for a quick visit?

On the safety guide, the structure is clear. I would suggest we add a simple do not list at the top, for example: do not re‑pack items with damaged packaging, do not leave chilled items out of cold storage beyond a set time, and do not guess expiry dates. That will help volunteers quickly understand the main risks.

For the doorstep script in A4, I like that it is short. One question: there is a line asking if the household has had any recent changes in health. That might feel a bit too personal for a quick delivery. Could we rephrase it to something more general, like asking how they are managing at home, without going into health details?

Good catch. To stay non‑clinical and within our remit, we could change that part to: how are things going for you at the moment, especially with food and day‑to‑day tasks. That keeps it open without asking about health conditions. We can also add a reminder in A4 that if someone raises serious concerns, we note it briefly and follow the escalation pathway rather than trying to solve it on the doorstep.

On privacy, we should make sure the script includes a short explanation of what we will and will not record. For example, that we use household codes, that notes are brief and non‑sensitive, and that information is only shared with the project team. That will align A4 with how we plan to use A6.

I can add that do not list to the top of the guide and keep the rest in simple bullet points. I will also include a short section on what to do if someone spots a potential issue during delivery, for example, a parcel left out too long, so that it is clear when to discard items.

The rephrased question sounds better. It feels more natural to ask how things are going rather than about health. I also like the idea of a clear reminder about escalation, so I know when to pass something on instead of trying to handle it myself.

For T5, I would suggest we keep the script to no more than three core questions plus a closing line. Something like: 1) how are things going for you at the moment, 2) is the food you are receiving working for you, and 3) is there anything making day‑to‑day tasks harder right now. Then a closing line about how they can reach out via partners if they need more support.

I like that structure. It keeps the conversation short and respectful. I will adjust T5 and A4 to reflect those three questions and the closing line, plus the privacy explanation that 534740 suggested.

On the safety guide, could we also add a short note about not discussing individual households in open areas, to reinforce confidentiality? It fits naturally with T3 and will remind people that safety also includes how we talk about residents.
Yes, I can add a short confidentiality reminder to the guide, linking it to how we use household codes rather than names. That should keep T3 aligned with our privacy approach.

Given the changes we have discussed, I think the food safety and hygiene guide now covers the essentials in clear language: key do not points, basic handling rules, what to do if in doubt, and a short confidentiality reminder. Unless anyone sees a major gap, I suggest we sign this off as the guide for the pilot and share it with all participants as part of T9.
Agreed, the guide feels clear and practical now. I am comfortable using it to brief volunteers and staff.

On the final script, I am happy with the three questions and the closing line. It feels like something I can say naturally at the door without taking too long. As long as we keep it to that length in A4, I am fine with using it from the dry run onwards.
From a logging perspective, the three questions also map neatly to three short note fields in A6, which will help keep records consistent without capturing sensitive detail.

To capture the decision: we will use the updated doorstep script with three core questions and a short closing line, plus a brief explanation of what we record and how we escalate concerns. I will finalise T5 and A4 accordingly and share them ahead of the briefing in T9.

threads.thread_goal: Set up tracking, labelling and logging tools before the dry run.

messages.text: I have put together a proposal for parcel and household labelling under T7, plus first drafts of the tracking and log templates in A5 and A6 for T8. The idea is: 1) each household gets a code like N1‑001, 2) each parcel label shows household code, route code, and delivery date, and 3) A5 tracks which households are on which route, while A6 captures delivery and outreach notes. Can you review this and flag any issues before we lock in the scheme?

The coding scheme looks straightforward. For A5, could we add a simple vulnerability flag that does not reveal details, for example, a single letter indicating the main referral route. That might help us later when we look at reach, without storing sensitive information.

From a privacy angle, the household code and route code on labels are fine as long as we do not include names or full addresses on A5 or A6. The mapping from codes to addresses should stay in a separate, restricted file. We should also keep the outreach notes column in A6 very short, focusing on practical points rather than personal history.

Looking at A6, I just want to check that filling it in will not slow down the route too much. Right now there are several columns. Could we keep it to date, route, household code, delivered yes or no, and a very short note field? Anything more detailed might be hard to complete between stops.

That makes sense. I can simplify A6 to those core columns and move any extra detail to an optional comments sheet that only the core team uses after the route, if needed. The main log will stay quick to complete at the doorstep.

On the labels themselves, we should make sure they are easy to read in the packing area. I would suggest we print the household code in larger font and keep the route code and date smaller. That will help packers quickly match parcels to the right household during staging.
Agree on the label layout. For T6, it will also help if the label is applied after the final checklist step, so we know the parcel is complete before we tag it with the household code.

On the vulnerability flag idea, I would keep it very broad, for example, a code for referral source only, such as C for community organisation, S for social work team, and H for health partner. That avoids labelling households by need type while still giving us some insight into reach.
Good suggestion. I will add a referral source column to A5 with those broad codes and no further detail. That should keep us on the safe side regarding privacy.
Thanks for simplifying A6. With the shorter list of columns, I am more confident I can keep it up to date during the route without delaying deliveries.
One more point: for the dry run in T10, could we include a column in A6 to note any issues with labels or tracking, so we can refine T7 and T8 before the full roll‑out?

Yes, I can add a small issues column specifically for the dry run, and we can later summarise those in A7. After the first week, we can decide whether to keep that column or move to a separate incident log only.

To summarise the scheme: 1) household codes like N1‑001, 2) parcel labels showing household code, route code, and date, with the code in larger font, 3) A5 tracking households, routes, and broad referral source codes, and 4) A6 logging date, route, household code, delivered yes or no, a short note, and a temporary issues column for the dry run. If everyone is comfortable with this, I suggest we adopt it as our standard labelling and tracking approach for the pilot.
That summary works for me. It should be easy to explain during the briefing and simple enough for volunteers to follow.
I am ok with using this scheme on the route. The labels and shorter log should be manageable in practice.

threads.thread_goal: Review dry run results and agree adjustments and next steps.

messages.text: We have completed the one‑week dry run with 6 households as part of T10. I have summarised the main issues in A7: 1) one route ran about 30 minutes late due to slow packing, 2) two parcels had labels that were hard to read, and 3) a couple of doorstep conversations took longer than planned. Overall, no food safety incidents and all deliveries were completed. Let us use this thread to review what we want to adjust before deciding whether to proceed with the full 6‑week roll‑out.

From the delivery side, the main challenge was the time spent at the door. A few conversations went beyond 5 minutes, which added up. The script in A4 is fine, but I think we need clearer guidance on how to close the conversation politely if it is running long.

On packing, we noticed that volunteers were double‑checking expiry dates even after sorting, which slowed things down. That suggests we need to reinforce the separation between the T2 sorting step and the T6 final check, so people trust that items reaching the packing table are already screened.

On labels and logs, A5 and A6 mostly worked, but we had two labels where the household code was smudged. That made it harder to match parcels to the log. We might need slightly better pens or pre‑printed stickers for the codes, especially if we scale up.

On the longer conversations, we could add a short closing line to A4, something like: I need to move on to the next delivery now, but thank you for your time. If you would like more support, here is how you can reach us. That gives you a natural way to wrap up without cutting people off abruptly.
That would help. A clear closing line makes it easier to manage time while still being respectful. I am happy to try that in the next round.

Agreed. For the full pilot, I will tighten T2 so that expiry checks are clearly part of sorting, and T6 will only include a quick final check for obvious issues. I will also schedule an extra 15 minutes at the start of each packing session to remind volunteers of the process.
That should help. I can also adjust the T6 checklist to highlight that expiry has already been checked in sorting, so packers know they are doing a quick confirmation rather than a full review.

For labels, I recommend we move to pre‑printed stickers with household codes and route codes for the full pilot, if budget allows. If not, at least we should standardise on thicker pens and a clear place on the parcel where labels go, to avoid smudging.

Given the limited budget, pre‑printed stickers for all parcels might be tight, but we could at least print sheets of household codes and route codes in advance and then stick them on manually. That would still reduce handwriting errors without a big cost.

From my side, pre‑printed codes would be great. During the dry run, I had to double‑check a couple of smudged labels against A6, which took extra time. Anything that makes the codes clearer will help keep the route moving.

On timing, if we implement the clearer separation between sorting and packing and add the closing line to the script, I think we can bring the route back within the planned window. We might also start packing 15 minutes earlier on busy days to build in a buffer.

Looking at A7 and the feedback here, the main issues seem manageable with these tweaks. We had no safety incidents, all 6 households received parcels, and the feedback captured in A6 was generally positive. From a community perspective, I do not see a reason to stop the pilot, as long as we implement the adjustments we have just discussed.
I agree. With the process tweaks, I am comfortable moving ahead with the full 6‑week pilot. It will be important that we keep using T11 to monitor weekly metrics and flag any new issues early.

From the tracking side, I am also comfortable proceeding. I will update A5 and A6 to reflect the label improvements and any extra columns we found useful during the dry run, then we can use them consistently for the rest of the pilot.
I am ok to continue as well, especially with the clearer closing line and better labels. The dry run showed that the route is doable with some fine‑tuning.

Let me summarise the agreed adjustments: 1) clarify T2 and T6 so expiry checks sit mainly in sorting, with a quick final check in packing, 2) add a clear closing line to the doorstep script in A4, 3) improve labels via pre‑printed or clearer codes under T7, and 4) start packing slightly earlier on busy days to build a buffer. With these changes, we will proceed with the full 6‑week pilot and use T11 to monitor weekly metrics and A7 to log any incidents or near‑misses. I will capture this in A8 as part of the end‑of‑pilot documentation later.
